configKeys.effect: How much one gemstone changes the SIZE: the Growth Gemstone multiplies generic.scale by it, the Shrinking Gemstone divides by it. A creature is only ever one step from its natural size — shrunk, natural or grown — so with the default the reachable sizes are x0.5, x1 and x2 and nothing further. The cap is the design: without it the gemstones would stack into arbitrarily huge mobs.

What one whole block of extra SIZE is worth in stats, as factor^(size-1). At the default of 1.5 a creature at twice the usual size is 1.5x, one at three times is 2.25x and Sif at 3.25 is 2.49x. The rungs are additive in size on purpose: three times as big should be worth 1.5 twice over. The bonus is derived from the size itself, so a creature that SPAWNED big earns it without a gemstone — but it only ever tops up to the species default times the multiplier and never stacks on a creature that is already stronger than that. Set to 1.0 to change size only and leave every stat alone.

Which ladder the stats climb, from util/SizeScaling. Both agree at double size (1.5) and part company past it: ADDITIVE counts whole blocks of extra size, so 3.0 is worth 2.25 and Sif's 3.25 is 2.49; MULTIPLICATIVE counts doublings, so 3.0 is 1.90 and Sif 1.99, and shrinking becomes the exact inverse of growing. There is no right answer — switch to compare in game.
Smallest NATURAL size a creature may have for the gemstones to work on it — the size it was born with, read from the attribute's base value, not the size it is now.

Largest NATURAL size a creature may have for the gemstones to work on it. Anything already bigger is out of their reach on purpose: an oversized wolf from a dungeon, or Sif from Grim Kingdoms, stays exactly as rare as it was found and can be neither grown further nor cut down to an ordinary size.

configKeys.defaultValue: max_health, attack_damage, movement_speed;1.25, jump_strength;1.0, step_height, armor
configKeys.effect: The attributes that follow the size, scaled by stat_factor as a top-up against the species default. An entry may carry a CAP after a semicolon: the furthest that attribute's multiplier may get from 1 in either direction, where 1.0 pins it (no scaling at all) and anything below 1 means no limit. Speed is capped at 1.25 because a mount reads MOVEMENT_SPEED straight through — LivingEntity.getRiddenSpeed, which wolf_mount overrides to exactly that value times its own multiplier — so a size-3.25 wolf at the full 2.49x reached 0.75 movement speed, outran chunk loading and snagged on every block edge, because at nearly a block per tick the collision arrives before the step-up does. Jump strength is pinned outright: a mount that launches is worse than one that does not jump higher. A creature that lacks an attribute skips it.

Let a creeper's blast follow its size, scaled by stat_factor. The explosion is the one stat that is not an attribute — Creeper.explodeCreeper reads a plain int field — so it is handled separately, by writing that field. At the defaults a grown creeper goes from 3 to 4 and a shrunk one down to 2, and a charged creeper still doubles on top. Rounding is chosen so the walk is reversible: growing floors, shrinking rounds, and 3 -> 4 -> 3 holds.

Chance that a naturally spawning creature comes out an odd size. Only MobSpawnType.NATURAL and CHUNK_GENERATION count — never a spawner, a spawn egg, a breeding or anything a command placed, because those are someone deliberately asking for a creature and getting a giant instead would be a nuisance rather than a surprise. 0 switches it off.
Of the creatures that come out odd, the share that come out SMALL rather than large. 0 makes every one of them a giant, 1 makes every one tiny.
Let every hostile creature (anything extending Monster) take part. Off means only extra_entities does.

Creatures that take part although they are not hostile, by entity id. Quark's Foxhound is here by default: a Nether wolf that already spawns down there and tames with coal, but it extends Wolf rather than Monster, so the hostile rule alone would pass it by. An oversized one is the closest thing to Sebi's 'nether dogs that are already +1' — the mob exists, it only needed a reason to be big.
Let the gemstones resize players too. Off by default: a shrunk player sees over no stair and a grown one suffocates in its own corridors.

Only allow resizing creatures that belong to the player holding the gemstone — any OwnableEntity whose owner UUID matches. A safety switch for shared servers; off by default so a giant creeper stays possible.
Refuse to grow a creature when its new hitbox would not fit where it stands. Without it Entity.refreshDimensions gives up looking for a free spot and the animal suffocates inside the ceiling.
Use up the gemstone on a successful change. Creative mode never consumes it, and a refused click never consumes it either.

Entity types the gemstones refuse to touch. The Ender Dragon ignores the attribute anyway (its sanitizeScale returns a hard 1.0F), but listing it turns a gemstone that silently does nothing into a readable refusal. Ids are validated with containsKey, because ENTITY_TYPE is a DefaultedRegistry and an unknown id would otherwise resolve to minecraft:pig.

configKeys.defaultValue: emerald block, 4 crimson wart blocks, 4 amethyst shards
configKeys.effect: The crafting recipe for the Growth Gemstone, in the same format custom_crafting_recipes uses: recipe_id;result_item;result_count;pattern;keys. Editable so the pack can re-price the gemstones without a new build. An empty string makes the gemstone uncraftable.

configKeys.defaultValue: emerald block, 4 warped wart blocks, 4 amethyst shards
configKeys.effect: The crafting recipe for the Shrinking Gemstone, same format as growth_recipe.

Chests that may contain a gemstone, as loot_table;chance. The chance is rolled once per chest and which of the two gemstones drops is an even 50/50. Applied through LootTableLoadEvent, so any mod's chest table can be added.

items.name: Growth Gemstone
items.notes: GemstoneItem with grows=true. Right-click a living creature to move it one step up: size x scale_factor, stats x stat_factor. Only works on a creature at its natural size or currently shrunk — a creature that is already grown is refused, which is the cap. Consumed on success unless the player is in creative or consume_item is off. Crimson icon with an engraved arrow pointing up, drawn from scratch by scripts/gen_gemstone_textures.py.

items.name: Shrinking Gemstone
items.notes: GemstoneItem with grows=false. The exact inverse: one step down, dividing size and stats by the same two factors. Used on a grown creature it removes the growth modifier and restores the creature's own numbers bit for bit. Warped-teal icon with an engraved arrow pointing down.

mixins: special_gemstones.CreeperExplosionRadiusAccessor (@Accessor on Creeper.explosionRadius, common side; the blast is a plain int field, not an attribute, and Explosion.radius is private final so it cannot be adjusted at detonation time either)
notes:
WHAT EXISTS: two items (vanillaplusadditions:growth_gemstone, vanillaplusadditions:shrinking_gemstone, both GemstoneItem extends Item), one interaction handler pair, one recipe reload listener, one loot-table listener. No block, no entity, no mixin, no packet, no client class.

THE SIZE IS THE VANILLA ATTRIBUTE. minecraft:generic.scale exists since 1.20.5 as a RangedAttribute("attribute.name.generic.scale", 1.0, 0.0625, 16.0).setSyncable(true) and is part of LivingEntity.createLivingAttributes(), so every vanilla living entity has it. EntityScaling never writes the base value; it adds one ADD_MULTIPLIED_TOTAL modifier and reads the base only to learn the creature's natural size.

THREE STATES, NOT A FREE SCALE. A creature is shrunk, natural or grown, and a gemstone moves it exactly one state. The state is not stored anywhere of ours: it IS the pair of permanent attribute modifiers vanillaplusadditions:gemstone_grown and vanillaplusadditions:gemstone_shrunk, detected with AttributeInstance.hasModifier(ResourceLocation). Permanent modifiers are saved in the entity's "attributes" NBT and synced to every tracking client, so the state survives saving, chunk unload and a restart with no data attachment (which would not reach the client anyway).

WHY MODIFIERS AND NOT setBaseValue: exact reversibility. Multiplying base values leaves rounding behind on every round trip and, far worse, overwrites the creature's own rolled numbers — a horse's health, movement speed and jump strength are randomised per animal, and those are the hidden stats that must survive being grown and shrunk again. Removing a modifier restores them bit for bit. addOrReplacePermanentModifier is used rather than addPermanentModifier, which throws IllegalArgumentException("Modifier is already applied on this attribute!") on a second add with the same id.

THE STATS FOLLOW THE SIZE, NOT THE GEMSTONE. util/SizeScaling offers two ladders and stat_curve picks: ADDITIVE is stat_factor^(size-1) (1.5 at size 2, 2.25 at 3, 2.49 at Sif's 3.25) and MULTIPLICATIVE is stat_factor^log2(size) (1.5 at 2, 1.90 at 3, 1.99 at Sif), which makes shrinking the exact inverse of growing and keeps very large creatures tamer. They agree at double size and part company past it.

PER-ATTRIBUTE CAPS EXIST BECAUSE OF MOUNTS. LivingEntity.getRiddenSpeed is the mount's speed, and wolf_mount overrides it to MOVEMENT_SPEED times its own multiplier — so the size bonus lands on the ride one to one. A size-3.25 wolf at the full 2.49x reached 0.75 movement speed: it outran chunk loading (measured in game, 36 fps down to 11) and snagged on block edges, because at nearly a block per tick the collision arrives before the step-up does. A cap after a semicolon in scaled_attributes limits how far one attribute may travel; 1.0 pins it. Speed is capped at 1.25, jump strength pinned outright. EntityScaling.refreshSizeStats runs on every EntityJoinLevelEvent as well as after a gemstone, so a creature that SPAWNED big earns the bonus with nobody having clicked it.

IT TOPS UP, IT NEVER STACKS. The target is the SPECIES default (DefaultAttributes.getSupplier) times the multiplier, and a creature already stronger keeps what it has: one ADD_VALUE modifier of max(0, default*m - base). Sif is the case this exists for — 350 health at size 3.25 would otherwise be handed another 2.5x on top, and a hand-tuned boss from another mod would be quietly rebalanced by us. Shrinking is the other way round, base*m - base, because there the point is to take something away. A multiplier of exactly 1 returns 0 without touching anything, or the top-up would drag a creature another mod deliberately WEAKENED back up to its species default.

IDEMPOTENT BY CONSTRUCTION: refreshSizeStats works out the modifier it wants, compares it with the one already on the attribute, and returns without touching anything if they agree — which is what makes running it on every entity join safe. Health is carried across as a FRACTION of max health, so a wounded animal stays proportionally wounded rather than being healed by a reload. Attributes the creature does not have are skipped: a cow has no attack damage, and only horses and their relatives roll a jump strength.

MIGRATION: beta.100 briefly put the step markers (gemstone_grown/gemstone_shrunk) on the stat attributes themselves. refreshSizeStats strips them on join, so anything changed with that build settles onto the new scheme by itself.

WHAT STAYS OUT OF REACH: a creature whose NATURAL scale is outside min_natural_scale..max_natural_scale is refused outright, in both directions. That is what keeps an oversized dungeon wolf or Sif unique — it can neither be grown further nor cut down to an ordinary size.

NOTHING HAS TO BE SYNCED OR REFRESHED. AttributeMap.onAttributeModified queues every syncable instance and ServerEntity broadcasts ClientboundUpdateAttributesPacket, so the client follows within a tick; LivingEntity.aiStep compares getScale() with its last applied value and calls refreshDimensions() itself, which is what moves the hitbox, the eye height and the passenger attach point.

WHY PlayerInteractEvent AND NOT Item#interactLivingEntity: Player.interactOn calls entity.interact(player, hand) FIRST and returns as soon as the entity consumed the click; only if it did not does it reach itemstack.interactLivingEntity. A tamed wolf, cat or axolotl toggles sit/stand on any unknown item, a horse mounts, a breedable animal eats — so an item hook would never fire on exactly the animals worth resizing. EntityInteract (and EntityInteractSpecific, which fires first when the click lands on a specific part of the hitbox) runs before all of it, via CommonHooks.onInteractEntity at the top of interactOn.

THE CANCELLATION RESULT MATTERS. The handlers cancel with InteractionResult.sidedSuccess(isClientSide), never with PASS: a PASS cancellation lets the client fall through to the use-item stage. Same trap the axolotl_guardian module documents for the water bucket. setCancellationResult and setCanceled are declared on the two subclasses, not on the abstract PlayerInteractEvent, so the shared helper takes the pieces rather than the event.

BOTH SIDES FIRE. The event runs client-locally in MultiPlayerGameMode.interact and server-side in Player.interactOn; everything that mutates is behind level.isClientSide(). Only the main hand is handled, otherwise the off-hand re-fires the same click.

REFUSALS, all with an action-bar message and the gemstone kept: the target is on denied_entities, the target is a player and allow_players is false, require_tamed is on and the entity is not an OwnableEntity owned by the clicking player, the creature is already one step out and cannot go further, its natural size is outside the reachable band, or the grown hitbox would not fit. The space check scales the CURRENT bounding box about the entity's feet and asks level.noCollision — Entity.refreshDimensions does try fudgePositionAfterSizeChange for a mob that grew, but gives up when there is no free spot, and the animal then suffocates in the ceiling.

THE CREEPER'S BLAST IS THE ONE STAT THAT IS NOT AN ATTRIBUTE. Creeper.explodeCreeper reads a private int field (3 by default, doubled while charged); Explosion.radius is private final, so ExplosionEvent.Start cannot adjust it either without cancelling and restarting the explosion, which re-fires the same event. The module writes the field through a mixin accessor instead, which also persists for free because vanilla saves it as ExplosionRadius in the creeper's NBT. Rounding is picked for reversibility: growing floors, shrinking rounds, so 3 -> 4 -> 3 and 3 -> 2 -> 3 both hold at stat_factor 1.5. It follows stat_factor rather than scale_factor so a grown creeper is a 4, one short of a charged creeper's 6.

THREE VANILLA ENTITIES IGNORE OR CAP THE ATTRIBUTE, by their own code, not ours: EnderDragon.sanitizeScale returns a hard 1.0F, Shulker.sanitizeScale caps at 3.0F, and Slime/MagmaCube size themselves from their own `Size` data value rather than the attribute. The dragon and the wither are on the default denylist so the refusal is a readable message instead of a gemstone that silently does nothing.

THE POINT OF THE PAIRING: wolf_mount only lets a wolf be ridden at generic.scale >= 2.0 (WolfMountRules.isLargeEnough, config eligibility.min_scale, default 2.0), and with the defaults NO naturally occurring wolf qualifies — the module was built around Sif from Grim Kingdoms, a plain minecraft:wolf on a spawn egg with scale 3.25. One Growth Gemstone on a tamed vanilla wolf is the first way to reach 2.0 in normal play. The reverse also holds: WolfMountRules.stillEligible is re-checked while riding, so shrinking a ridden wolf below min_scale dismounts the rider.

THE RECIPES COME FROM THE CONFIG. Own-item recipes belong to their own module by project convention, so they exist exactly as long as this module is enabled — but the shape is two config strings in the same format custom_crafting_recipes uses, parsed by the shared util/ConfiguredRecipes. That parser was lifted out of CustomCraftingRecipesModule for this module; there is deliberately one parser and one format. Reason for the config: the pack owner wanted the price to be chosen by a player, not fixed in a release. An empty string makes that gemstone uncraftable. The shipped default is Sebi's design — a block of emerald cored with four nether/warped wart blocks and four amethyst shards, nine emeralds and thirty-six warts per gemstone. The Nether half is his argument too: it is the compact dimension, so size magic belongs there, with crimson reading as bigger and warped as smaller.

CHEST LOOT GOES THROUGH LootTableLoadEvent, the project's route for editing a foreign loot table, not a datapack JSON. One pool per configured table, one roll, a LootItemRandomChanceCondition for the chance, and the two gemstones as equally weighted entries. The pool carries a name because NeoForge's LootTable.addPool throws RuntimeException on a duplicate pool name, and the event fires again on every /reload — the name is both label and guard.

THE DENYLIST USES containsKey FIRST. BuiltInRegistries.ENTITY_TYPE is a DefaultedRegistry whose get() never returns null: an unknown id silently comes back as minecraft:pig, so a typo would protect pigs instead of reporting itself. Same trap mob_drops documents.

THE TEXTURES ARE ORIGINAL ART. scripts/gen_gemstone_textures.py draws both 16x16 icons from geometry and two colour ramps; no vanilla texture is read, recoloured or copied, so they share no pixels with emerald.png (see docs/internal/BACKLOG.md, "Abgeleitete Vanilla-Texturen aufloesen"). One silhouette, two palettes, the way the four wolf_armor_*.png icons work. They are distinguishable twice over: by hue and by an arrow pointing up vs one pointing down engraved in the pavilion, so colour-blind players can still tell them apart. The hues follow the recipe rather than being picked freely — crimson for the gem cut around nether wart, warped teal for the one cut around warped wart, the same red-means-bigger, blue-means-smaller logic the recipe carries. The arrow is CUT IN, which is a lighting problem: an engraving is a relief with the light reversed, so the groove is shadowed along its top and left edge and catches the light along its bottom and right; the shadowed rim is four steps down the gem's own ramp from the facet under it, so the cut reads equally deep on the bright table and the dark tip. The core stays bright because a real groove loses contrast as it deepens and 16 pixels have none to spare. The script has a --check mode.

STANDALONE JAR: the vpa_special_gemstones jar registers its items unconditionally, because StandaloneModuleBootstrap initialises regardless of the enabled flag — with enabled=false the items exist but no click, recipe or loot does anything.

NOT VERIFIED IN GAME YET (2026-09-27): compiles and passes Checkstyle. Worth checking specifically that a tamed wolf does not sit down instead of growing, that the size survives a world reload, that a grown wolf satisfies wolf_mount, that a second growth is refused, and that a horse grown and shrunk again has exactly its original speed and jump strength.

BORN THE WRONG SIZE: FinalizeSpawnEvent rolls natural_spawns.chance (default 2%) on NATURAL and CHUNK_GENERATION spawns only, and sizes the mob one step — 70% large, 30% small by default. The result is an ordinary grown or shrunk creature: same marker a gemstone leaves, same size-derived stats, and a Shrinking Gemstone walks it back. Spawner, egg, breeding and command spawns are excluded on purpose, because those are someone deliberately asking for a creature. EntityScaling.applyAtSpawn shares every rule the gemstones follow (denylist, natural-size band, one step) except the space check: the spawner has already placed the mob, and leaving it at ordinary size is a better failure than refusing the spawn.

QUARK'S FOXHOUND is in natural_spawns.extra_entities by default. It is the Nether wolf Sebi asked about: it already spawns down there and tames with coal, but it extends Wolf rather than Monster, so the hostile rule alone would pass it by. Naming it gives 'nether dogs that are already +1 and have better stats' without a new mob — the animal existed, it only needed a reason to be big.
oneLiner: Two emerald-priced gemstones that make the creature you right-click one size bigger or smaller — stats and all, once each way — and the first way to grow a wolf big enough to ride.

shortDescription: Adds two emerald gemstones that move the creature you right-click one step up or down in size, scaling its stats with it, via the vanilla generic.scale attribute.
